questions.question: What is the relationship between a Docker image and a container?
options: An image is an immutable package; a container is a runnable instance with runtime configuration and a writable layer
An image is a running process and a container is its source repository
They are two names for the same mutable filesystem
A container always contains a complete guest operating-system kernel
questions.explanation: The image supplies read-only filesystem layers and metadata. Docker creates a container from that image plus runtime settings, isolation, and a container-specific writable layer.

questions.question: Why copy dependency manifests before application source in a Dockerfile?
options: It encrypts the source tree
A source-only edit can preserve the cached dependency-install layer
It makes every build ignore the lockfile
It puts development dependencies outside every image automatically
questions.explanation: Docker invalidates a changed layer and dependent layers after it. Isolating stable dependency inputs lets frequent source changes begin invalidation later.

questions.question: What does a multi-stage build change about the final image?
options: Every file from every stage is merged automatically
The final stage can copy selected artifacts while leaving the builder toolchain behind
The final image becomes mutable
Build cache is disabled
questions.explanation: Each FROM starts a stage. A later stage copies only required artifacts, so compilers, source, and development dependencies need not ship at runtime.

questions.question: A database writes only to its container writable layer. What happens when that container is removed and replaced?
options: Docker attaches the old writable layer automatically
The data is copied into the image registry
The old writable layer is removed and the replacement starts without that data
The data becomes a named volume
questions.explanation: The writable layer belongs to one container. Durable database files need storage whose lifecycle is independent, such as a managed volume with an explicit backup plan.

questions.question: When is a bind mount a better semantic fit than a named volume?
options: When a host tool and the container must both edit a specific host path
When the workload must avoid host-path coupling
When data must disappear on stop
Whenever an image should contain a secret
questions.explanation: A bind mount deliberately exposes a daemon-host path. That is useful for source editing, but it couples the container to host layout and permissions.

questions.question: What is true when no Docker memory limit is configured?
options: The container is automatically limited to 512 MB
The container can use memory allowed by the host kernel and may contribute to host OOM pressure
The process cannot allocate swap
The image size becomes the memory limit
questions.explanation: Containers have no resource constraints by default. Operators should measure workload demand and set limits that protect the host without creating avoidable OOM kills.

questions.question: Why use a BuildKit secret mount instead of ARG or ENV for a build credential?
options: Secret mounts make the credential temporarily available to one build instruction without persisting it in the final image
ARG values are always encrypted in image history
ENV values disappear before the next layer
Secret mounts publish the credential to the registry
questions.explanation: Docker documents build arguments and environment variables as inappropriate for secrets because they can persist. A secret mount exposes the value only for the consuming instruction.
